abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework to analyze how automation and AI-driven productivity advances affect long-run economic growth. The authors find that despite substantial productivity acceleration from automation, output gains are surprisingly modest due to 'weak links'—tasks with low elasticity of substitution—which constrain how quickly capital can be reallocated across the economy. By 2040, output is only 4% higher than baseline, and by 2060 still only 19% higher, suggesting automation's growth benefits are dampened by complementarities and adjustment frictions in production networks.
keyFindings: Weak links (elasticity of substitution less than one) substantially slow the economy's ability to translate automation productivity gains into output growth.
Despite acceleration in AI capabilities, cumulative output gains by 2040 reach only 4% above baseline, indicating significant adjustment constraints.
By 2060, the long-run output gain from the growth acceleration remains modest at 19%, suggesting structural impediments to rapid capital reallocation.
The model demonstrates that productivity improvements in individual tasks do not translate linearly to aggregate growth when task complementarities are present.
